note: Pressure scenarios for the leadership assessment. Responses are NOT scored into the radar — they produce a separate qualitative 'under pressure' reading. There is no correct answer.
intro: Four situations security leaders actually meet. Choose the response closest to what you would genuinely do — not the one that sounds best.

stabilise.name: Stabilise first
stabilise.reading: Under pressure you reach first for ground: slow the situation down, name what is known, and hold a steady centre while others react.
stabilise.strength: You keep the room from spiralling, and decisions made from that ground tend to hold.
stabilise.edge: Steadiness can read as slowness to people already moving. Say what you are doing and why, or the pause looks like a stall.

adapt.name: Adapt first
adapt.reading: Under pressure you reach first for movement: change the shape of the problem, trade a constraint, find the path that is actually open.
adapt.strength: You rarely get stuck, and you find options other people have written off.
adapt.edge: Constant re-shaping can leave the team without a fixed point. Name what will not move, so the flexibility reads as choice rather than drift.

connect.name: Connect first
connect.reading: Under pressure you reach first for people: get the right parties in the room, surface what each actually needs, and move the situation through relationship.
connect.strength: Your decisions get adopted, because the people who have to live with them helped shape them.
connect.edge: Consultation costs time you may not have. Decide in advance which calls are yours alone to make.

envision.name: Reframe first
envision.reading: Under pressure you reach first for the wider frame: what this incident means, what it reveals, what it should change.
envision.strength: You convert pressure into direction, and the same failure rarely arrives twice.
envision.edge: The wider frame does not close today's ticket. Pair the reframe with a concrete next action inside the hour.

scenarios.title: The blocked deal
scenarios.text: A customer security review is blocking your largest deal. The deadline is Friday. Your CTO is in an all-hands and Sales has already promised the questionnaire will be back today.

options.text: Stop the promising. Establish what can truthfully be answered today, answer that, and put a dated commitment against the rest.
Find another route to the same outcome — a compensating control, a scoped exception, a conditional sign-off that unblocks Friday.
Get Sales and the customer's security reviewer into one call and find out which answers actually matter to them.
Answer it, then treat this review as the specification for the trust story you should have had ready before the deal existed.

scenarios.title: The 48-hour vulnerability
scenarios.text: A critical vulnerability is disclosed in a dependency you ship. Engineering says a safe fix takes three weeks. Your largest customer is asking for 48 hours.

options.text: Establish the real exposure before anyone commits to a date — reachability, blast radius, what is actually exploitable in your deployment.
Ship mitigation now and the fix later — pin, patch at the edge, or disable the affected path while the real work proceeds.
Call the customer yourself, tell them what you know and do not know, and agree a schedule you can actually meet.
Handle it, then ask why a three-week fix was the fastest option available and change that.

scenarios.title: The control nobody uses
scenarios.text: A control you introduced six months ago is being routed around. Engineering has a shared workaround. Nobody raised it with you.

options.text: Re-state the requirement and the reason behind it, then hold the line consistently until it is met.
Assume the control is wrong for the workflow and redesign it around how the team actually works.
Ask the engineers who built the workaround what the control costs them — and why they did not tell you.
Treat the silence as the finding, not the workaround, and address why security problems are not surfacing to you.

scenarios.title: The board question
scenarios.text: In a board meeting a director asks, without warning, whether the company is secure. The honest answer is complicated and you have about ninety seconds.

options.text: Give the plain position: what is protected, what is not yet, and what you are doing about the gap.
Reframe the question into one you can answer usefully — which risks are accepted, and by whom.
Find out what prompted the question before answering it — the concern behind it is the real question.
Answer briefly, then use the moment to set the standing measure the board should be tracking every quarter.
